I looked for a VolumeQueueLength alarm in account 012345678901_1 (us-east-1) so I could pull more metrics, and didn't find one there. Everything below is worked out from your numbers.

## What the numbers show

- **The volume is nowhere near its limits.** It's running at 900 of 6,000 IOPS (15%) and 40 of 250 MiB/s (16%). Neither limit is holding it back.
- **Each I/O is taking longer.** Average queue length roughly equals IOPS × average time per I/O, so time per I/O ≈ queue length ÷ IOPS. If the queue grows while IOPS falls, each I/O must be slower. With made-up numbers: a queue of 2 at 3,000 IOPS is about 0.7 ms per I/O, and a queue of 10 at 900 IOPS is about 11 ms. Plug in your real values.
- **The IOPS drop is probably an effect, not the cause.** An application with a roughly fixed number of I/Os in flight finishes fewer per second when each one is slower.
- **I/O size looks normal.** 40 MiB/s ÷ 900 ≈ 45 KiB per I/O. That's well under 256 KiB, the size above which gp3 counts one I/O as more than one. Compare it with your normal size and read/write mix anyway; a change there means the workload changed.

## Should you add IOPS?

Probably not. Provisioned IOPS raises the ceiling, but it doesn't make each I/O on gp3 faster. Two checks could change that answer:

1. **Short bursts.** One-minute averages hide bursts within the minute. An average of 900 could be 6,000 for a few seconds and almost nothing the rest of the time, which fills the queue. Check the volume's `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` and `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` metrics. A value of 1 during the window means the workload tried to go past what's provisioned, so more IOPS or throughput (or spreading out the bursts) would help. A value of 0 means it won't.
2. **The instance limit is shared.** The 12,000 IOPS / 750 MiB/s instance limit covers every EBS volume attached to the instance, not just this one. It's only "not the limit" if all attached volumes together stay below it. Check the instance's `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` metrics. If they show 1, the fix is the instance size or type, or moving volumes, not this volume's IOPS.

## Is it AWS-side? Can't tell yet

The checks that came back clean only catch hard failures, not slowness:
- Volume status and `VolumeStalledIOCheck` catch I/O that isn't completing at all. Yours is completing, just slowly.
- AWS Health shows announced, broad problems. Trouble with a single volume often never appears there.
- An empty FIS list only rules out a test you ran on purpose.

So EBS isn't cleared, but nothing points at it either. These checks would separate the two:

| Check | Points to AWS | Points elsewhere |
|---|---|---|
| EBS-side write time per I/O (`VolumeTotalWriteTime` ÷ `VolumeWriteOps` for each period) vs. the OS view (`iostat` await) | High on the EBS side | Normal on EBS but high in the OS: the queue is inside the instance (filesystem, I/O scheduler, CPU) |
| I/O size, read/write mix, rate of forced (sync) writes, any deploy or batch job when it started, all vs. normal | No change | Changed: the application is the cause |
| Volume history | Not recently created or modified | Created from a snapshot recently without Fast Snapshot Restore: data loads from S3 the first time each block is read, so latency is high, IOPS low, and every check green. Or a size/performance change still finishing (`DescribeVolumesModifications`) |
| Other volumes on the same instance and in the same Availability Zone | Unrelated volumes slow down in the same minute | Only this volume is affected (that still doesn't rule out a single-volume AWS problem) |

If all of these come out on the AWS side (both exceeded checks at 0, high write time on the EBS side, no workload change, and no snapshot loading or modification in progress), that's what a degraded volume on AWS's side looks like. In that case:
- Open an AWS Support case with the volume ID and the exact time window.
- Move the data to a new volume: snapshot it and create a new one, using Fast Snapshot Restore or reading every block once first. Don't pay for IOPS this volume isn't using.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### EBS VolumeQueueLength up while IOPS down
**Description:** gp3 volume queue length increased while IOPS fell to ~900 (of 6,000 provisioned) and throughput sat at ~40 MiB/s, indicating higher per-I/O latency. Exact start time not provided by user.
**Time:** unknown

## Findings

### Hypothesis: Sub-minute bursts exceeding provisioned IOPS/throughput
**Description:** 1-minute averages of 900 IOPS could hide bursts to 6,000 that fill the queue. Check VolumeIOPSExceededCheck / VolumeThroughputExceededCheck: 1 means more IOPS/throughput (or smoothing bursts) would help; 0 means it won't.
**Cascades to:** symptom-queue-length-rise

#### Gaps
- **Analysis based only on user-supplied numbers:** No VolumeQueueLength alarm exists in account 012345678901_1 (us-east-1) and no volume ID was identified, so no CloudWatch metrics (exceeded checks, write time, instance EBS checks) were pulled to confirm any hypothesis.

### Hypothesis: Shared instance EBS limit reached across attached volumes
**Description:** The 12,000 IOPS / 750 MiB/s instance limit is shared by all attached EBS volumes. Check InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck / InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck; if 1, the fix is instance size/type or moving volumes, not this volume's IOPS.
**Cascades to:** symptom-queue-length-rise

#### Gaps
- **Analysis based only on user-supplied numbers:** No VolumeQueueLength alarm exists in account 012345678901_1 (us-east-1) and no volume ID was identified, so no CloudWatch metrics (exceeded checks, write time, instance EBS checks) were pulled to confirm any hypothesis.

### Hypothesis: Workload change or in-instance queuing
**Description:** Compare EBS-side write time per I/O (VolumeTotalWriteTime ÷ VolumeWriteOps) with OS iostat await: normal on EBS but high in the OS means queuing in the filesystem, I/O scheduler or CPU. Also compare I/O size, read/write mix, sync-write rate and any deploy/batch job at onset vs normal.
**Cascades to:** symptom-queue-length-rise

#### Gaps
- **Analysis based only on user-supplied numbers:** No VolumeQueueLength alarm exists in account 012345678901_1 (us-east-1) and no volume ID was identified, so no CloudWatch metrics (exceeded checks, write time, instance EBS checks) were pulled to confirm any hypothesis.

### Hypothesis: Snapshot lazy-load or volume modification in progress
**Description:** A volume recently created from a snapshot without Fast Snapshot Restore loads blocks from S3 on first read: high latency, low IOPS, all checks green. A size/performance modification still finishing (DescribeVolumesModifications) can look similar.
**Cascades to:** symptom-queue-length-rise

#### Gaps
- **Analysis based only on user-supplied numbers:** No VolumeQueueLength alarm exists in account 012345678901_1 (us-east-1) and no volume ID was identified, so no CloudWatch metrics (exceeded checks, write time, instance EBS checks) were pulled to confirm any hypothesis.

### Hypothesis: Degraded volume on the AWS side
**Description:** Indicated if both exceeded checks are 0, EBS-side write time is high, there is no workload change, and no snapshot loading or modification is in progress. Unrelated volumes in the same AZ slowing in the same minute would also point here.
**Cascades to:** symptom-queue-length-rise

#### Gaps
- **Analysis based only on user-supplied numbers:** No VolumeQueueLength alarm exists in account 012345678901_1 (us-east-1) and no volume ID was identified, so no CloudWatch metrics (exceeded checks, write time, instance EBS checks) were pulled to confirm any hypothesis.
